lessons.title: Quadrats, transects and abundance
lessons.summary: Use random coordinates to avoid choosing favourable quadrat locations.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Use random coordinates to avoid choosing favourable quadrat locations. Count consistently and repeat widely. Mean count divided by quadrat area gives density; density times habitat area estimates population. Uneven distribution makes this an estimate, not an exact census.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: A transect investigates distribution along a gradient. Use quadrats at measured intervals and measure the relevant abiotic factor. Repeat transects and standardise counting rules. A correlation with light does not rule out variation in moisture or soil.

keypoints: Use random coordinates to avoid choosing favourable quadrat locations.
A transect investigates distribution along a gradient.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Carbon and water cycles
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms. Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon dioxide. Decomposition returns mineral ions to soil; combustion releases stored carbon dioxide. Matter is recycled rather than created.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Evaporation and transpiration transfer water to air, condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns it. Runoff and soil movement return water to rivers and oceans. Materials cycle, whereas energy eventually dissipates to surroundings and is not recycled in the same way.

keypoints: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms.
Evaporation and transpiration transfer water to air, condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns it.

Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Biodiversity, pollution and land use
lessons.summary: Biodiversity is the variety of species.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Biodiversity is the variety of species. It supports stable food webs and resources such as food and potential medicines. Human population growth and consumption increase waste, including sewage, fertilisers, toxic chemicals, smoke and acidic gases.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Farming, building, quarrying and waste disposal can destroy habitats. Deforestation reduces habitats and releases carbon through burning or decay. Peat stores partly decomposed carbon; draining or extracting it damages habitats and releases carbon dioxide. Explain both ecological effects and the demands driving land use.

keypoints: Biodiversity is the variety of species.
Farming, building, quarrying and waste disposal can destroy habitats.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Climate and maintaining biodiversity
lessons.summary: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature. Changing climate can alter distribution, migration and food availability and increase extinction risk. Distinguish long-term trends from daily weather, and consider uncertainty and time span when interpreting evidence.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Breeding programmes, protected habitats, restoration, hedgerows and field margins can support biodiversity. Reducing deforestation, emissions and waste can reduce damage. Compare ecological benefits with cost, housing or food-production needs to make a reasoned judgement.

keypoints: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature.
Breeding programmes, protected habitats, restoration, hedgerows and field margins can support biodiversity.

checks.why: Weather varies while climate uses long-term data

ms: It can restore habitats and biodiversity / carbon storage.
It may reduce agricultural land or income.

lessons.title: Decomposition, compost and biogas
lessons.summary: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature. Warming increases enzyme activity up to an optimum; excessive heat denatures enzymes. Aerating compost supports aerobic decomposition, returning useful nutrients to soil.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Milk decay can be followed through falling pH as microorganisms produce acids. Compare time for a defined change at controlled temperatures. Anaerobic decay in biogas generators produces methane fuel. A pH-change rate is a proxy, not a direct bacterial count.

keypoints: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature.
Milk decay can be followed through falling pH as microorganisms produce acids.

lessons.title: Trophic levels and biomass efficiency
lessons.summary: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers. Biomass pyramids compare dry mass at a stated time. Less biomass reaches higher levels because not all is eaten, some is undigested and respiration releases carbon dioxide.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100. A transfer of 600 kg from 8000 kg is 7.5%. Energy transfers to surroundings rather than being destroyed. Do not assume every ecosystem has the same efficiency or confuse dry biomass with organism number.

keypoints: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.
Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100.

lessons.title: Food security and sustainable production
lessons.summary: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food. Population growth, climate, pests, disease, conflict and costs influence supply and access. Fishing quotas and suitable net sizes allow populations to reproduce. Increased production alone does not guarantee fair distribution.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Controlled livestock conditions can reduce energy used in movement and warming but raise welfare concerns. Fermenters produce fungal mycoprotein; modified crops may improve nutrition or resistance. Evaluate output, resource use, emissions, welfare and cost rather than assuming a single solution works everywhere.

notes.title: Mycoprotein and improved nutrition
notes.html: Fusarium fungus can grow aerobically on a carbohydrate feed in a fermenter, supplying protein-rich food. Controlled oxygen, temperature and nutrient supply support growth; harvested biomass is processed for food. Genetically modified crops can also improve nutritional content, such as enhanced vitamin precursors, but suitability depends on the dietary problem and local evidence.

keypoints: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food.
Controlled livestock conditions can reduce energy used in movement and warming but raise welfare concerns.

Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

ms: Controlled temperature / movement can increase growth efficiency.
Welfare, disease or resource-use concerns must be considered.
